To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the response signature of the prostate-specific antigen (PSA) is not the same for all patients, that it depends on the PSA level, that the response signature can be predicted by using the PSA level and the PSA doubling time (PSA DT), and that the response signatures are similar for the two most widely used anti-androgen drugs, flutamide and bicalutamide.
the PSA response to treatment can be described as a series of signatures, and that the PSA response signatures can be predicted by the initial PSA level and the treatment.
The PSA response signature is a useful tool to identify patients with prostate cancer that are likely to benefit from ADT.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the analysis of PSA (prostate-specific antigen) response signatures, i.e. the time course of PSA levels following the initiation of a new treatment.
the use of a new methodology to analyse PSA response signatures in prostate cancer patients.
the analysis of the PSA response signatures of patients with prostate cancer.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
there is insufficient evidence to suggest that the PSA test should be used for the routine screening of men for prostate cancer.
the PSA response signatures are an important tool for the evaluation of the response of prostate cancer patients to the treatment with androgen deprivation therapy.
the use of PSA as a tumor marker in prostate cancer is not as simple as it may seem, but that PSA is a very useful marker in the management of prostate cancer.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the PSA response signatures are a useful tool to predict response to therapy in patients with prostate cancer.

the PSA response signature is the most accurate predictor of biochemical recurrence (BCR) in men undergoing definitive radiotherapy for prostate cancer, and that this signature can be used to identify men at low, medium, and high risk for BCR after radiotherapy.
the response of prostate-specific antigen (PSA) to androgen ablation therapy (AAT) in men with metastatic hormone-sensitive prostate cancer can be predicted from the baseline PSA level.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the use of PSA response signatures is a useful tool in the management of men with prostate cancer.

the use of a PSA response signature to predict the outcome of patients with metastatic castration-resistant prostate cancer (mCRPC) is feasible, and that the use of this signature is more accurate than the use of PSA kinetics alone.
the use of a single PSA response signature to predict prostate cancer outcomes is not appropriate.
